chapter_summary:
When an application or service fails on a Linux system, it can disrupt critical operations. The first step in troubleshooting is to determine if the service is actually running. Use `systemctl status <service_name>` to check its current state. If it's `failed` or `inactive`, the next logical step is to examine its logs. For `systemd`-managed services, `journalctl -u <service_name> -xe` provides detailed output, including recent log entries, error messages, and the exact command that failed. Many applications also maintain their own log files, typically found in `/var/log/` (e.g., `/var/log/nginx/error.log`, `/var/log/mysql/error.log`). Always consult both `journalctl` and application-specific logs, as they often provide complementary information. Common mistakes include only checking `journalctl` and missing application-specific debugging output, or vice-versa.

Configuration errors are a very frequent cause of application failures. Syntax errors in configuration files (e.g., `nginx.conf`, `httpd.conf`, `my.cnf`) can prevent a service from starting or cause it to behave unexpectedly. Many services offer a configuration test command (e.g., `nginx -t`, `apachectl configtest`, `mysql --help`). Always run these tests after making changes to avoid downtime. Permission issues are another common culprit. If a service runs as a specific user (e.g., `nginx` as `www-data`), it must have appropriate read/write permissions to its configuration files, data directories, and log files. Use `ls -l` and `namei -l` to inspect permissions and ownership, and `chmod`/`chown` to correct them. For example, if Nginx cannot read its web root, it will return 403 Forbidden errors. Verify the user the service runs as (often found in its `systemd` unit file or configuration) and ensure that user has access to all necessary resources.

For deeper analysis of a running or failing process, `strace` and `lsof` are invaluable. `strace` traces system calls and signals, showing exactly what a program is doing at a low level. `sudo strace -p <PID>` attaches to a running process, while `strace -o output.log <command>` runs a command and logs its system calls to a file. This can reveal missing files, permission denied errors, or unexpected network interactions. For example, if an application fails to open a file, `strace` will show `open("filename", O_RDONLY) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)` or `ENOENT (No such file or directory)`. `lsof` (list open files) lists all open files and network connections by processes. `sudo lsof -i :80` shows all processes listening on or connected to port 80. `sudo lsof -p <PID>` shows all files opened by a specific process. This is excellent for identifying resource leaks, unexpected file access, or processes holding onto network ports.

When troubleshooting custom scripts (e.g., Bash, Python), adding debugging statements (`set -x` in Bash, `print()` in Python) can help trace execution flow. For compiled applications, if available, using a debugger like `gdb` (GNU Debugger) can provide extremely detailed insights into program execution, memory, and variables, though this is typically for developers rather than system administrators. Resource contention, such as memory exhaustion or CPU spikes, can also lead to application failures. Tools like `top`, `htop`, `free`, and `vmstat` (covered in more detail in Chapter 11.5) help identify these. Always consider the wider system context: Is the disk full? Is the network saturated? Are there enough file descriptors available (`ulimit -n`)? A methodical approach, leveraging logs, configuration checks, and process inspection tools, is crucial for effectively resolving application and service failures.

screens.title: Application & Service Failures
screens.subtitle: Systematic troubleshooting for Linux services, scripts, and compiled applications

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn a practical, methodical approach to diagnosing application and service failures on Linux. We begin with confirming service state using systemctl, then move to log analysis with journalctl and application-specific logs, and finally to deeper inspection with tools like strace and lsof. You will see how configuration syntax errors and file permission problems are common causes, and how small fixes such as running a configuration test or correcting ownership can restore service availability. A hands-on scenario walks through a Python Flask app managed by systemd that fails because its script file is unreadable; you will practice checking status, reading journals, verifying file permissions with ls -l and namei -l, and fixing the permission with chmod. This focused chapter ties together quick checks and deeper process inspection so you can escalate appropriately: logs and config tests first, then strace and lsof if necessary. By the end you will have a repeatable checklist to reduce Mean Time To Repair when an important service stops working.

keyIdea.title: Start with state and logs, escalate to process inspection
keyIdea.text: Confirm service state, inspect systemd and application logs, then use strace or lsof when logs and config checks do not reveal the root cause.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Application & Service Failures
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Application & Service Failures

A practical guide to diagnosing failing services. Learn the sequence: confirm state, read logs, validate configuration and permissions, then inspect processes and resources for deeper faults. This reduces guesswork and restores services faster.

Diagnostic Snapshot
State
Use systemctl status to confirm running, failed, or inactive states and view the unit command and exit code.
Logs
Combine journalctl -u with application logs in /var/log to see complementary messages and stack traces.
Inspect
Use strace and lsof for low-level system calls and open file/socket information when higher-level logs are insufficient.
Explore Key Topics
State & Units
Confirm service state with systemctl and inspect the unit file for user, working directory, and ExecStart details.
Logs & Tests
Use journalctl -u -xe and application log files, and run service-specific config tests to spot syntax errors early.
Process Tools
Attach strace or run lsof to reveal missing files, denied permissions, or sockets held by a process.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Practical skills to diagnose and inspect failing services

narration.text: These objectives describe the hands-on skills you will practice. First, you will systematically diagnose failures by confirming service state and following a checklist that moves from logs to process inspection. Second, you will learn to use systemd's journalctl and application-specific logs together so you can correlate timestamps and find the exact failing command or stack trace. Third, you will use strace and lsof to observe system calls and open resources, which is essential when logs are silent or misleading. Fourth, you will be able to detect configuration syntax and permission errors quickly by running service-specific config tests and inspecting ownership and access with ls -l and namei. Each objective ties to practical commands and small experiments so you can practice safely on a lab VM. Understanding these skills shortens troubleshooting time and reduces unnecessary restarts. You will be asked to demonstrate each step in a guided lab that simulates a real service failure so you internalize the sequence: state, logs, config, permissions, then process-level inspection.

keyIdea.title: Sequence for effective troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Work from high-level signals to low-level inspection: confirm state, read logs, test configuration, check permissions, then inspect process behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Deeper inspection, debugging, and resource awareness

narration.text: This second set of objectives extends the practical checklist into deeper inspection and debugging techniques. You will learn to troubleshoot common application issues such as misconfigured syntax, missing files, permission problems, and resource contention that causes intermittent failures. You will practice basic debugging for scripts by enabling trace modes or printing values, and understand when to escalate to a native debugger for compiled binaries. Additionally, you'll learn to check system context: disk space, file descriptor limits, and memory or C P U spikes that can cause otherwise healthy services to fail. These skills matter because many failures are caused by environmental constraints rather than buggy code, and fixing environment issues avoids repeated incidents. The lab ties these objectives into a guided repair of a Flask application started by systemd so you can practice both diagnosis and repair in a controlled setting.

keyIdea.title: From symptom to root cause
keyIdea.text: Combine log analysis, configuration validation, permission checks, and resource inspection to find whether the fault is code, config, or environment.

screens.title: Confirming service state with systemctl
screens.subtitle: Check unit state, recent exit codes, and unit details before deeper debugging

narration.text: The first, simplest diagnostic step is to confirm whether the service is actually running. Use the command systemctl status followed by the service name to see its current state, active status, and often the last few log lines. You also get the process ID and the exact ExecStart command, which can reveal a mispointed binary or a wrong working directory. If the unit shows failed or inactive, inspect the unit file for the User, Group, WorkingDirectory, and ExecStart fields; mismatches between the unit and file-system permissions are frequent causes of startup failure. A common misconception is assuming a failed service must be the application code; often the unit configuration or an environmental change prevents the process from executing. For example, a service configured with User=www-data but with a WorkingDirectory owned by root and unreadable by www-data will never start correctly. Confirming the state also tells you whether to proceed with log reads or to attempt a controlled restart. Keep this as your first check so you avoid chasing the wrong hypothesis and so your next steps are targeted and effective.

keyIdea.title: Start with systemctl status
keyIdea.text: systemctl status gives state, recent logs, PID, and unit configuration clues that often point to configuration or permission issues before you escalate.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Service State

Confirming service state with systemctl

Use the unit status to decide the next diagnostic step: read logs, test config, or inspect processes.

Quick checklist
  • Run systemctl status <service> to read state, PID, and recent log output.
  • Note the unit's User, WorkingDirectory, and ExecStart to spot misconfiguration.
  • If state is failed, inspect journalctl -u next rather than immediately restarting.
  • Look for non-zero exit codes or repeated restarts that hint at config or permission errors.
Key Takeaway

Use systemctl status as your first, low-risk diagnostic to gather facts before changing service state.

Example & unit snippet
$ systemctl status my_app
● my_app.service - My Cohortia Flask App
   Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/my_app.service; enabled)
   Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Mon 2026-01-01 12:00:00; 3s ago
  Process: 12345 ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 my_app.py (code=exited, status=203/EXEC)
The status line shows the exit code and the exact ExecStart command. A status like 203/EXEC suggests the binary or script couldn't be executed — often a permission or path issue.
Common mistake
Restarting repeatedly without checking the unit or logs can mask the root cause and make logs rotate away. Gather evidence first.

screens.title: Reading systemd logs with journalctl
screens.subtitle: Use journalctl -u and flags to see context and extended errors

narration.text: Journalctl is the systemd journal viewer and is often the best place to look after systemctl shows a failure. The command journalctl -u service-name -xe prints recent entries for that unit with expanded detail and a priority-based ordering. The -x flag includes additional explanatory text when available, and -e jumps to the end of the log, which is useful to see the most recent failure messages. When you run journalctl, look for timestamps and the exact command line that failed; the journal often records the exit code and the reason systemd stopped the process. A common trap is relying solely on journalctl and missing application-specific logs where stack traces or detailed errors appear; another trap is only checking application logs and missing systemd-level environment information like environment variables or unit limits. When you see an error in the journal, record the timestamp and search application logs for the same timeframe. If the journal is noisy, combine it with --since and --until to narrow the window. Always correlate journal messages with unit configuration and application logs before changing configuration or code.

keyIdea.title: Use journalctl for structured systemd logs
keyIdea.text: journalctl -u <service> -xe shows the systemd journal context; combine it with app logs and timeframe filters to locate errors precisely.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › journalctl

Reading systemd logs with journalctl

journalctl gives timestamped, structured logs from systemd-managed services. Use filters to focus on the failure window.

Common journalctl commands
# show recent entries for a unit with extra info
journalctl -u my_app -xe

# limit to a time range
journalctl -u my_app --since "2026-01-01 11:59" --until "2026-01-01 12:05"

# follow in real time
journalctl -u my_app -f
Use --since and --until to isolate the failure window. -f is useful when restarting to watch new messages as the service attempts to start.
Example snippet and interpretation
Jan 01 12:00:00 host systemd[1]: Starting My Cohortia Flask App...
Jan 01 12:00:00 host python3[12345]: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/opt/my_app/my_app.py'
Jan 01 12:00:00 host systemd[1]: my_app.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
Jan 01 12:00:00 host systemd[1]: my_app.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
This combination shows both the Python stack trace and systemd's recorded exit: correlate the timestamp and the exact file path to check file permissions or ownership next.
Pro tip
If the journal lacks application detail, check /var/log/ for richer stack traces before moving to strace.

screens.title: Application-specific logs in /var/log
screens.subtitle: Why application logs complement the systemd journal

narration.text: Many applications maintain their own log files in /var/log and these files often contain richer, application-level context such as stack traces, S Q L errors, or web server request failures. For instance, nginx writes error entries to /var/log/nginx/error. log and a database like MySQL keeps its own error log under /var/log/mysql. These application logs can show configuration parsing failures, runtime exceptions, or request-level details that journalctl may not capture. A common mistake is checking only journalctl and missing application-debug output, or checking only app logs and missing unit-level environment or exit information. When you investigate a failure, record the timestamp from the journal and then look in the application log for entries at the same time; this often reveals the full stack trace or a config parse error. Use ls -l to check ownership of the log file and parent directories because a service must be able to write to its own logs. If logs are missing, confirm that the application is configured to write logs to disk and that disk space and file descriptor limits allow logging. Application logs and systemd logs together provide the full picture needed for most fixes.

keyIdea.title: Look for detail in application logs
keyIdea.text: Application logs often contain full stack traces and error details that the systemd journal does not record; always correlate timestamps across both sources.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Application Logs

Application-specific logs in /var/log

Always check both systemd journal and the application's own logs to get complete diagnostic details.

Common log locations
  • /var/log/nginx/error.log for nginx errors and config parse messages.
  • /var/log/mysql/error.log or /var/log/mysqld.log for database startup and runtime errors.
  • Application-specific paths configured in the service or application settings.
If application logs are empty, verify the service user can write to the log directory and that log rotation didn't move entries away.
Example: check file ownership and existence
$ ls -l /var/log/nginx/error.log
-rw-r----- 1 www-data adm 12345 Jan  1 12:00 /var/log/nginx/error.log

# trace path permissions
$ namei -l /var/log/nginx/error.log
f: /var/log/nginx/error.log
 d root root /
 d root root var
 d root root log
 d root root nginx
 - www-data adm error.log
namei -l shows ownership for each path element; missing execute bits on a parent directory prevents traversal even if the file itself is readable.
Key Takeaway
Correlate timestamps between the journal and app logs to see both system-level context and application-level errors.

screens.title: Testing configuration and avoiding syntax errors
screens.subtitle: Run built-in config checks before restarting services

narration.text: Configuration errors are a frequent cause of service failure. Many daemons provide a syntax check command that should be run after any edit to configuration files. For example, nginx offers nginx -t, apache provides apachectl configtest, and many database servers include a configuration test or print helpful help output. Running these tests catches mismatched braces, invalid directives, or deprecated options early, and prevents downtime caused by reloading a broken configuration. A common mistake is to edit the live file and reload without testing; if the test fails, the service may refuse to restart or may start with default settings. When a configuration test fails, read the test output carefully: it typically points to a file and a line number. Fix the line, re-run the test, and only then reload or restart. Also ensure that the service user has read access to included configuration files and any referenced certificates or keys; config tests can pass but the running service may still fail if it cannot read a referenced file at runtime. Automated pre-deploy checks in CI or a quick manual test are inexpensive ways to avoid production outages.

keyIdea.title: Validate config before restart
keyIdea.text: Use the daemon's built-in config test to detect syntax or include errors before reloading or restarting a service.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Config Tests

Testing configuration and avoiding syntax errors

Run configuration tests after edits so you don't reload a broken config into production.

Useful commands
  • nginx -t — checks Nginx configuration syntax and file includes.
  • apachectl configtest — validates Apache configuration before restart.
  • mysql --help or mysqld --validate-config (varies by distribution) — look for database config test options.
Example: nginx syntax error
$ nginx -t
nginx: [emerg] unknown directive "server_nam" in /etc/nginx/nginx.conf:45
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test failed
The output locates the file and line number so you can correct the typo and re-run the test. Only reload after tests pass.
Key Takeaway
A quick config test prevents many service outages and points directly to the offending line or include.

screens.title: Permissions and ownership troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Use ls -l and namei -l to trace access problems

narration.text: Permission problems are one of the most frequent causes of application failure. A service that runs as a particular user must be able to read its configuration, open data files, and write to logs. Start with ls -l to inspect file ownership and mode bits, but remember that directory execute bits control traversal and read bits control listing. To see all parent ownership and permissions for a path, use namei -l; it breaks the path into components so you can detect a missing execute bit on a parent directory that prevents access even if the file itself is world-readable. A typical example is a web root owned by root with restricted permissions; the web server user cannot read files and returns 403 errors. Another common misdiagnosis is to change only the file permissions when the real issue is the parent directory or an SELinux context — if SELinux is enabled it can also deny access. After identifying the problem, use chown to set the correct owner and chmod to adjust permissions. Make smallest necessary changes to avoid over-permissive settings. Confirm by running the service as the intended user when possible to reproduce the access problem before applying the fix.

keyIdea.title: Trace the full path for access checks
keyIdea.text: Use namei -l in addition to ls -l to reveal permission problems on parent directories that block access for the service user.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Permissions

Permissions and ownership troubleshooting

Verify ownership and directory traversal to ensure the service user can access required files.

Commands to inspect access
$ ls -l /opt/my_app/my_app.py
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 234 Jan 1 11:59 /opt/my_app/my_app.py

$ namei -l /opt/my_app/my_app.py
f: /opt/my_app/my_app.py
 d root root /
 d root root opt
 d root root my_app
 - root root my_app.py
If the file is owned by root and service runs as www-data, change ownership with sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /opt/my_app and restrict permissions appropriately.
Example scenario
A web server returns 403. You check the webroot and find the directory lacks the execute bit for the web server user. After running sudo chmod o+x /var/www/html and confirming ownership is correct, requests succeed. Always prefer minimal permission changes that grant exactly the access required.
Common mistake
Setting files to 777 hides the real access model and can create security problems. Fix ownership and fine-grained permissions instead.

screens.title: Using strace to follow system calls
screens.subtitle: Trace opens, reads, and permission errors to find missing or inaccessible files

narration.text: Strace records the system calls a process makes and is invaluable when logs do not explain why a program fails. You can attach to a running process with sudo strace -p PID or run a command and write output to a file with strace -o output. log command. The output shows calls like open, stat, connect, and the return values; failures like ENOENT or EACCES immediately reveal missing files or permission denials. For example, an entry open("/opt/my_app/my_app dot P Y file", O_RDONLY) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied) points directly to an unreadable file that the process tried to open. Use strace judiciously: it adds overhead and can produce a lot of data, so narrow the scope by tracing a short run or filtering system calls. Strace requires appropriate privileges to attach to processes you don't own, so use sudo. A common misconception is that strace is only for developers; sysadmins often use it to discover missing libraries, incorrect file paths, and unexpected network activity that logs miss. Always combine the strace evidence with journal and application logs to build a full picture before applying fixes.

keyIdea.title: Read system call errors
keyIdea.text: Strace shows low-level failures like ENOENT or EACCES at the moment a process attempts an operation, making root causes obvious.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › strace

Using strace to follow system calls

Trace system calls to see the exact operation that failed and its errno response.

Common usage
# attach to a running PID
sudo strace -p 12345

# run and capture calls
sudo strace -o /tmp/strace.log python3 /opt/my_app/my_app.py
Filter with -e trace=open,read,write or use -f to follow forks. Remember strace requires privileges for other users' processes.
Interpreting output
open("/opt/my_app/my_app.py", O_RDONLY) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)
stat("/etc/my_app/config.yml", {st_mode=...}) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
connect(3, {sa_family=AF_INET, sin_port=htons(3306)}, 16) = -1 ECONNREFUSED (Connection refused)
Each line shows the call and the kernel error. Use the returned errno to target the fix: create missing files, fix permissions, or resolve network access issues.
Misconception
Strace is not destructive but can slow processes. Use it in a controlled window and prefer targeted traces to reduce noise.

screens.title: Using lsof to find open files and sockets
screens.subtitle: Find which process holds a port or a file handle

narration.text: Lsof lists open files for processes and is exceptionally useful for identifying port conflicts, file descriptor leaks, or which process holds a filesystem object. Use sudo lsof -i :80 to see what is listening or connected on port 80, or sudo lsof -p PID to list all files a process has open. When troubleshooting a failed web server that says port already in use, lsof reveals the PID and command holding the port so you can decide whether to stop that process or reconfigure your service. Lsof also helps detect resource leaks: if a process shows thousands of open files, that indicates a file descriptor leak and suggests investigating the application's open/close logic. Note that lsof output includes file descriptor types such as REG for regular files and TCP for network sockets, helping you distinguish resource types. A common misconception is that lsof changes system state; it is read-only. Combine lsof results with ps or systemctl status to identify the unit controlling the process and with strace to see what operations the process performs on those files or sockets. This combination pinpoints leaking or conflicting resources without restarting services blindly.

keyIdea.title: Identify who holds what
keyIdea.text: lsof maps processes to open files and sockets so you can find port conflicts and resource leaks quickly.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › lsof

Using lsof to find open files and sockets

lsof reveals which processes hold files or network ports so you can resolve conflicts or leaks.

Common lsof commands
# show processes using port 80
sudo lsof -i :80

# list files held by a PID
sudo lsof -p 12345

# find deleted files still held open
sudo lsof | grep deleted
Use lsof to detect leftovers like deleted files still consuming disk because a process holds the descriptor open, or to detect binding conflicts before changing service ports.
Example output
COMMAND   PID   USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
nginx    2345  www-data  6u  IPv4  12345      0t0  TCP *:http (LISTEN)
python   3456  www-data  3u  REG   8,1  12345   567 /opt/my_app/log.txt
This shows nginx listening on port 80 and a Python process holding a log file. Use the PID to correlate with systemctl or ps to decide how to proceed.
Pro tip
Combine lsof with grep and ps to script checks that detect port conflicts during deployments.

screens.title: Debugging scripts and compiled applications
screens.subtitle: Trace scripts with verbosity and reserve gdb for compiled binaries

narration.text: When the failing component is a script, inexpensive trace techniques often reveal the problem. For Bash, enable set -x near the top or run the script with bash -x to print each command as it executes; for Python, adding print statements or running with increased logging shows the execution path and variable values. These approaches let you see where the script diverges from expected behavior. For compiled applications, a debugger like gdb provides source-level inspection of variables, stack frames, and memory, which is often necessary for deep defects but is generally used by developers. A common misconception is that print-style debugging and gdb are interchangeable; they serve different needs. Use print or trace for quick flow inspection and to capture high-level failures, and use gdb when you need to inspect memory, registers, or backtraces at the point of crash. When debugging in production, be careful: verbose print logs can leak sensitive information and impact performance. Prefer reproducing the issue in a controlled environment or using targeted logging statements that reveal only the necessary state. Keep a rollback plan in case increased logging affects service performance.

keyIdea.title: Choose the right debug tool
keyIdea.text: Use trace prints for scripts and gdb for compiled code; prefer controlled environments to avoid performance and security side effects in production.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Script & Binary Debug

Debugging scripts and compiled applications

Use simple traces for scripts and a debugger for native binaries when source-level inspection is required.

Script techniques
# Bash: enable execution trace
set -x

# Python: add basic logging
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)
logging.debug('starting handler')
Tracing prints the execution flow so you can see the failing statement and input values quickly.
Compiled applications
Use gdb to get a backtrace and inspect variables at the crash point. This is developer-focused and requires symbol information. When system administrators need to gather evidence, capture core dumps or run gdb in a controlled debugging session rather than instrumenting production processes live.
Caveat
Avoid leaving verbose debug output enabled in production; it may impact performance and expose sensitive data.

screens.title: Resource contention and wider system checks
screens.subtitle: Look beyond the app: disk, memory, CPU, and file descriptor limits

narration.text: Application failures can be caused by resource contention rather than code errors. Before assuming the application is buggy, check memory and C P U usage with top or htop, view free memory with free, and check input and output activity with vmstat or iostat. Disk full conditions cause unexpected behavior — services may fail to write logs or temporary files and crash. Also check file descriptor limits with ulimit -n and ensure the service's unit file sets appropriate LimitNOFILE if needed. A process may continue running while failing to serve requests because it cannot open new sockets or files. Another subtle problem is too-low process limits or cgroup constraints applied by the unit file. When you suspect resource exhaustion, collect evidence over time with top or vmstat and correlate spikes with service errors in the journal. A common misconception is to restart the service immediately; this can clear transient resource indicators and make diagnosis harder. Instead capture snapshots of usage and then address the underlying bottleneck — increase limits, adjust memory usage, or offload work — so the fix prevents recurrence.

keyIdea.title: Check the environment
keyIdea.text: Resource shortages or low limits often cause failures; inspect memory, CPU, disk, and file descriptor limits before changing application code.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Resource Contention

Resource contention and wider system checks

Measure system resources and limits before concluding an application bug is the cause of failure.

Commands to inspect resources
top or htop        # CPU and memory
free -h             # memory summary
vmstat 1 5          # short-term IO and CPU stats
df -h               # check disk usage
ulimit -n           # current file descriptor soft limit
If ulimit is too low, services may exhaust file descriptors; adjust LimitNOFILE in the systemd unit or increase ulimit for the service user where appropriate.
Scenario example
A database service runs but refuses new connections under load. top shows high memory usage and lsof -p shows thousands of open sockets. The root cause may be a runaway query or leaking connections; investigate queries and tune connection pooling rather than restarting repeatedly.
Key Takeaway
Collect resource usage evidence and adjust limits or capacity to prevent recurring failures tied to contention.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: repairing a Flask app permission error
screens.subtitle: Follow a repeatable sequence to diagnose and fix a permission-caused startup failure

narration.text: This lab simulates a real failure: a Python Flask app managed by systemd fails to start after an update and the journal shows a generic error. Start by checking systemctl status my_app to confirm the unit is failed and note the exit code. Next run journalctl -u my_app -xe and look for PermissionError or file access messages. With a timestamp from the journal, inspect the application file and its path with ls -l and namei -l to discover if the service user lacks read or execute permission. In the provided scenario a faulty chmod 000 made the script unreadable. To reproduce locally, run sudo -u www-data Python three /opt/my_app/my_app dot P Y file to see the same permission error as the unit. Once identified, fix ownership and permissions with sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /opt/my_app and sudo chmod 644 /opt/my_app/my_app dot P Y file, then sudo systemctl restart my_app. Verify success with curl localhost:5000 and re-check journalctl for clean startup messages. If issues persist, attach strace to the process or run strace -o /tmp/strace. log Python three /opt/my_app/my_app dot P Y file to capture the failing open call. This sequence — status, journal, ls/namei, reproduce as service user, fix permissions, restart, verify — is repeatable for many permission-related failures.

keyIdea.title: A repeatable lab sequence
keyIdea.text: Status → journal → inspect paths → reproduce as service user → fix ownership/permissions → restart → verify (use strace if necessary).

Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Lab Walkthrough

Lab walkthrough: repairing a Flask app permission error

Use the lab steps to practice the checklist and tools on a controlled example service failure.

Starter files (place under /opt/my_app)
# my_app.py
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/')
def hello_world():
  return 'Hello, Cohortia!'

if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000)

# /etc/systemd/system/my_app.service
[Unit]
Description=My Cohortia Flask App
After=network.target

[Service]
User=www-data
Group=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/opt/my_app
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 my_app.py
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Fault injection & diagnosis
  1. Make the script unreadable: sudo chmod 000 /opt/my_app/my_app.py
  2. Restart the unit and run: systemctl status my_app and journalctl -u my_app -xe
  3. Inspect ownership and traversal: ls -l /opt/my_app/my_app.py and namei -l /opt/my_app/my_app.py
  4. Reproduce as service user: sudo -u www-data python3 /opt/my_app/my_app.py
  5. Fix and verify: sudo chmod 644 /opt/my_app/my_app.py && sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /opt/my_app && sudo systemctl restart my_app && curl localhost:5000
Key Takeaway
Reproduce the error as the service user and inspect path permissions before applying fixes. This avoids guesswork and ensures the fix is targeted.

narration.text: Remember these core concepts as quick reference while troubleshooting. First, systemctl is the primary control point to check a service's state and unit details. Second, journalctl retrieves structured systemd logs; combine it with application logs in /var/log to get both system and application context. Third, configuration tests catch syntax errors before you restart a service, saving downtime. These three ideas form the backbone of a fast, reliable approach to resolving many service failures: confirm state, read logs, and validate configuration. Keep this checklist in mind and practice it until each step becomes a quick habit; this will reduce unnecessary restarts and make your debugging more surgical. Key Concepts — Diagnostics

A short set of compact reminders to guide quick triage.

systemctl
Control and inspect systemd units; it shows state, PID, and unit configuration used for diagnosis.
journalctl
Query systemd journal entries for a unit; use -xe and time filters to isolate failure messages.
Application Logs
Look under /var/log for application-specific errors and stack traces that journalctl may not include.
Summary

Confirm state, correlate journal and app logs, and run config tests before moving to process-level inspection tools like strace and lsof.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Tools & Remedies
screens.subtitle: Diagnostics tools and common remedies to retain

narration.text: A second set of concise reminders focuses on tools and common remedies. First, configuration errors frequently break service startup — always run the service's config test after edits. Second, permission issues are common and often fixed by adjusting ownership and permissions or correcting parent directory traversal; namei -l helps reveal parent ownership. Third, process-level tools like strace and lsof expose system calls and open resources when logs are inconclusive. Keep these three practical points in mind: test configs, verify permissions for the service user, and use strace/lsof to reveal low-level failures or resource leaks. These tools together give you a clear path from symptom to fix. Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts — Tools & Remedies

Practical reminders for the tools and fixes you will use most often.

Configuration Errors
Syntax or include errors often prevent services from starting; run the daemon's config test to catch them before reload.
Permission Issues
Incorrect ownership or missing execute bits on parent directories block service access; use ls -l and namei -l to diagnose and chown/chmod to fix.
strace & lsof
Use strace for system call errors and lsof to see open files and sockets; together they reveal missing resources or leaks.
Final takeaway

Work top-down: confirm state, read logs, validate config and permissions, then use strace and lsof to inspect process behavior and resources.
